newsitem.title: FRANCE: French public pay offer runs straight into flak.
newsitem.headline: French public pay offer runs straight into flak.

text.p: The French government, confronted by a possible strike, offered a 2.8 percent pay rise over two years to millions of public employees on Tuesday, but ran straight into flak.

The Communist-led CGT trade union broke the news of the 1997-98 offer after meeting Civil Service Minister Dominique Perben and said the proposals ignored a key demand from unions for a payment to make up for a pay freeze in 1996.

"What is important in the face of this kind of attitude is that employees make themselves heard loud and clear," the CGT said in a statement, adding that unions would meet in the evening to consider their response.
A Civil Service ministry official declined to comment but said Perben would hold a news conference at the end of the day (1700 GMT).

The 1996 civil service pay freeze was one of several union gripes behind crippling public sector strikes in late 1995 and the CGT said Perben had made it clear there was "no question" of making up for the 1996 freeze in the latest pay round.

Unions had warned in advance that they would fight any offer which failed to make at least "a gesture" to compensate for the loss of purchasing power last year, and that their response could include a strike in March.
Perben is meeting the unions one-by-one to present an offer covering millions of civil servants in central administration, teachers, health services staff and local authority employees.

"Is this the kind of framework in which the minister asks about the possibility of opening 'negotiations'?" the militant CGT said. "Negotiate what? A fall in purchasing power? New widespread losses due to the spreading-out (of the pay rise) envisaged?"

"The minister's announcement is a non-event. It was expected and is part of a policy which attacks purchasing power, public employment and the public service in the forced march of the convergence criteria (for European monetary union)," it said.

Pierre Avignon, head of the moderate white-collar CGC union, said last Wednesday that unions wanted negotiations but would consider a strike if they got a unilateral offer which fell short of their demands.

Jean-Pierre Gualezzi, head of the Unsa union grouping, said in an interview in the newspaper Les Echos on Tuesday that the union meeting later in the day was likely to result in a one-day strike call.

"(The government) forgets that the civil servants, and more globally the population concerned by its wage policy, represent a fifth of the working population and were behind the strikes of November-December 1995," he told the newspaper.
Civil servants also staged a one-day strike last October 17 over pay and government plans to cut their number by nearly 6,000 this year under the 1997 budget.

The strike was followed by about a third of civil servants, according to the civil service ministry, and unions held off on follow-up action after Prime Minister Alain Juppe signalled that pay talks could be reopened.

The latest stand-off comes a day before a rail strike called by the CGT and a protest rally by the Socialist CFDT union against government reforms which they say amount to a "break-up" of the SNCF railway network, threatening jobs and the rail monopoly.
